subject: Out-of-state investing — what to outsource, what you can't
preheader: 4 jobs you keep · 3 you delegate · The #1 OOS-investor failure mode (it's not the PM)

marketSnapshot.headline: Out-of-state investing — the jobs that can't be outsourced
marketSnapshot.body: Investing remotely is how investors in expensive coastal markets access affordable cash-flowing properties in the Midwest and Southeast. Done well it works. Done casually it loses money. The discipline: certain jobs MUST stay with you (the investor) even when you're 2000 miles away. Outsourcing those is the single biggest predictor of OOS-investor failure.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Rehabbed · existing PM · ready to rent
dealSpotter.body: Property in a B-tier neighborhood with an established local PM (5+ years), recently rehabbed, inspected. Sellable to an out-of-state investor because all the hard work is done. The premium for turnkey: maybe $8-12k more than the comparable distressed property, but you skip the rehab risk, contractor-finding, and 4-month vacancy that would otherwise eat that delta. Worth it for OOS investor #1 or #2.

Higher-yield C-tier property in an older urban neighborhood. The paper cap rate is real, but the property requires active management — block-by-block variation in neighborhood quality, older systems, tenant base needing more hand-holding. For an in-state investor with a property manager, this works. For an OOS investor first or second deal, the gap between paper cap and real return is wide enough to be painful.

Property with paper cap of 10.6%. The reality from local investors: real-world vacancy 18-24% (not 8%), bad-debt 4-7%, capex 18-22% rather than the typical 8-10% reserve. The 10.6% paper cap drops to 6.4% real for an absentee owner. Only worth pursuing if you have boots-on-the-ground.

qa.question: I live in CA. The math doesn't work locally. How do I OOS-invest without losing my shirt?
qa.answer: Four jobs you cannot outsource. (1) Underwriting — you do the math, not a sales agent or turnkey provider. Their incentives are wrong. (2) Picking the metro — research the state landlord laws, eviction timelines, and 5-year demographic trends. Don't take an agent's word for 'this is a hot market.' (3) Hiring the PM — interview at least 3 before signing. Ask for references AND specifically the addresses of properties they currently manage so you can drive-by (or have a friend drive-by) to verify condition. (4) Setting the operating budget — you decide what reserves are reasonable. Three jobs you SHOULD outsource: (1) Boots-on-the-ground tasks (showings, maintenance coordination, tenant placement). (2) Legal compliance (state-specific lease forms, security deposit handling, fair housing process). (3) Bookkeeping (Schedule-E-ready statements monthly). The #1 OOS-investor failure mode is outsourcing underwriting to the turnkey provider's pre-built model. That model is rarely the math you'd accept if you'd run it yourself.
